resources.string: Turn this phone into a receiver that feeds live aircraft data to ADS-B Exchange.

An RTL-SDR USB receiver. It plugs into the phone\'s USB-C port, directly or through an adapter or hub. The SDR stick itself runs warm, like any USB radio: leave a little room for air around it and its adapter, for example by raising the phone a few millimetres off the surface.
A 1090 MHz antenna, by a window or outside, as high as you can.
Power, for feeding around the clock: a USB-C hub with charging, or a wireless charger plugged into a wall adapter (a laptop\'s USB port can\'t power one reliably).

ADS-B Exchange receives the aircraft messages this phone hears, with a feeder ID that marks this as a phone feeder. With stats on, every few seconds it also receives the list of aircraft being tracked and their signal strength, for this feeder\'s statistics. With MLAT on, it also receives this phone\'s precise location, the antenna altitude and your feeder name, which MLAT needs to work out aircraft positions. ADS-B Exchange\'s public MLAT map lists feeders by name; with privacy off, it also shows your feeder at an approximate location, rounded to about 1 km, never the precise one. Privacy is on to start with. The app sends the precise location to no one but ADS-B Exchange.

1. Connect the SDR to this phone\'s USB-C port. Use a USB-C hub with charging to keep the phone powered.\n2. Attach the antenna and put it by a window, as high as you can.\n3. When Android asks to open this app, tick \"Always\" and tap OK. Feeding starts on its own.

Feeding resumes on its own once the battery is below 40 °C. Keep the phone out of direct sun and somewhere air can reach it.

Feeding and its stats can use several GB of data a month, so they pause on mobile data. They resume on their own when the phone is back on Wi-Fi. To feed over mobile data, turn it on in Settings.
The receiver stopped 5 times in 15 minutes. Check the SDR\'s cable and adapter, then try again or unplug the SDR and plug it back in.

Not charging, and the battery is running down. If it\'s on a wireless charger, plug the charger into a wall adapter rather than a laptop or other USB port, check the phone sits centred on it, and give it some airflow. Or use a USB-C hub with charging.
Running on battery. The SDR drains it quickly; keep the phone plugged in through a USB-C hub with charging.

The battery is warmer than usual (40 °C or more). Feeding doesn\'t normally do this: it\'s usually direct sun, a hot spot, or a wireless charging pad, which warms a phone more than a cable charger. Batteries kept on charge all the time last longer when kept cool.

On battery, Android cuts the feeder off from the internet for long stretches once the screen has been off a while, and some phones stop it altogether. To keep it feeding, tap Allow background running, then in the app\'s settings choose Battery and Unrestricted (on some phones: Don\'t optimise).
Tip: if your phone can limit charging to 80%, turn that on. It\'s much kinder to a battery that\'s plugged in all the time.

Open on the ADS-B Exchange map
Optional, but worth adding: it\'s how you\'ll find your feeder on ADS-B Exchange\'s Leaderboard and MLAT maps. Names are only used when MLAT is on.
MLAT is off, so this name isn\'t sent to ADS-B Exchange. Turn on MLAT to use it.
Multilateration: nearby feeders time the same signals so ADS-B Exchange can locate aircraft that don\'t broadcast their position. Needs a precise receiver location.
Hide my location on the public MLAT map

Still takes part in MLAT. Off, ADS-B Exchange\'s MLAT map shows your feeder at an approximate location (rounded to about 1 km). On, it shows no location, though your feeder name can still appear in its lists.
The antenna is within about 15 m of this phone
MLAT uses the phone\'s location as the antenna\'s. If the antenna is on the roof and the phone isn\'t, enter the antenna\'s position manually under Receiver location.

When the SDR is plugged in and after the phone restarts.

What ADS-B Exchange\'s own feeders send alongside the feed. Without it this feeder gets no statistics, and doesn\'t appear on the leaderboard or in the Feeder Hub. Sends the aircraft list every 5 seconds: about 1–10 GB a month, depending on how busy the sky is.

Off: feeding pauses whenever the phone isn\'t on Wi-Fi, so it doesn\'t use your data allowance (feed and stats together: several GB a month, more at a busy spot). Mobile mode always feeds over mobile data.
If this phone can\'t reach ADS-B Exchange for 15 minutes, hears no aircraft for 2 hours, or its battery runs down while it\'s on a charger.
\"auto\" suits most setups, or a value in dB such as 43.9.
Power an amplifier through the antenna cable (bias tee)

Only for an amplifier at the antenna that takes its power through the cable, with an SDR that can supply it (such as the RTL-SDR Blog V3 and V4). Without it, such an amplifier passes little or no signal. Leave it off otherwise: about 4.5 V on the antenna socket can damage an antenna or splitter that shorts it. The ADS-B Exchange stick doesn\'t need it. The amplifier adds a little to the power the feeder uses (about 0.1–0.5 W); on a charger it makes no difference.

Having trouble? Ask on ADS-B Exchange\'s Discord server. If you\'re asked for diagnostics, send them privately rather than in a channel: they include this feeder\'s ID and the receiver log, but not its location.
Using an amplifier powered through the antenna cable, and seeing few or no aircraft? Turn on "Power an amplifier through the antenna cable" under Feeding.
Your history starts the first time this phone feeds ADS-B Exchange. Everything it contributes from then on adds up here.

Sync pairs and MLAT messages help ADS-B Exchange locate aircraft that don\'t broadcast their own position.
Counted on this phone while it\'s connected to ADS-B Exchange. Clearing the app\'s data resets it.
The furthest aircraft heard in each direction since %1$s. Short spokes show where buildings or terrain block the antenna.
Builds up as aircraft are heard. Not recorded in mobile mode.
It starts again from now, for example after you\'ve moved the antenna. The rest of your history stays.

Move the antenna, give the numbers a few seconds to settle, then measure. Higher is better: near a window, away from metal and other electronics. Measure spots one after another, because traffic changes through the day.
Start the receiver first: the coach measures what it hears.

Compares the feeder with and without its wake lock (which keeps the phone from sleeping), about 20 minutes each, an hour in all. Start it, turn the screen off and leave the phone alone: only screen-off time counts. On a charger it shows whether feeding holds up; on battery (above 40% to start), the power used as well. Feeding carries on throughout.
Measuring %3$s (%1$d of %2$d): %4$d of %5$d minutes so far

Counter: the battery\'s own charge meter, the more accurate figure where the phone has one. Readings: the average of the power readings every 10 s. Both are measured only on battery. Stalls: times the app didn\'t run for over a minute, because the phone slept. Dropped: radio samples readsb couldn\'t keep up with. Bad-sync: above 0, MLAT stopped trusting this feeder\'s timing. The last run repeats the first, to show any drift during the test.

A safety stop: the battery reached 45 °C. That\'s rare and usually comes from direct sun or a wireless charging pad, not from feeding. Feeding resumes on its own once the battery has cooled.
